verdict.note: Every layer earns its place: CLI arg adapter, public-surface gateway, authenticated loopback transport, sidecar authorization/lease broker, in-browser dispatcher, draft authority. The double AGENT_PUBLIC_COMMAND_SET check (operation-gateway in CLI + /api/tools in sidecar) is intentional defense-in-depth, documented in code. Real risk is temporal: lease/revision checks in the sidecar are evaluated against the last pushed snapshot (browserLeaseContext.currentRevision = snapshot.draftVersion), then the browser re-validates expectedRevision — correct, but a stale snapshot between inspect and apply widens the blind window the revision check must catch.

verdict.note: Lean path reusing path D's machinery — correct by construction. One asymmetry: the recovery effect's catch writes node error state via updateProject directly instead of returning a WorkflowRunResult through the executor, so recovery failures bypass the RUN_FAILED error taxonomy and any correlationId/runId context; the node ends in 'error' with a hand-built message rather than a normalized code. Also the resume effect requires userApiKeys.length>0 — a project opened before keys hydrate (or with zero keys) silently never resumes until a later state change re-fires the effect; recoveryTasks dedupe means a failed first attempt is not retried within the session.

verdict.note: Thin but honest layering: connector manifest + skill doc + the shared CLI pipeline. Two real observations: (1) workbuddy.auth only runs ensureFlovart — if services are already up it returns local-ready without proving the browser Workflow link specifically (ensureResponse checks browserConnected via getLocalStatus, so it does — verified); (2) unAuth unconditionally reports success even when nothing was ever connected — semantically correct per the no-account model but indistinguishable from a real logout to WorkBuddy's connector state machine.
